Long vowels occur only in the word-initial syllable, e.g., <bäpa> /bɐ:pɐ/ ‘father’ but not *<bapä> (Lowe, 1975). [Graetzer, Hajek & Fletcher 2012, p. 91:] In the CV1.CV2 words, such as <gapu> /gapu/, V1 is prosodically prominent (associated with regular non-final lexical stress) and V2 is both prosodically weak and word-final.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word; secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables after it (third, fifth..), but never on the final syllable. Long vowels are confined to the stressed initial syllable. Graetzer and colleagues' own acoustic corpus (three female speakers, citation-form CVCV words, F0-peak-based prominence labelling) confirms the initial syllable as the prominent one ('main stress was word-initial in these data', 2014 and 2016 papers).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per Lowe 1975 as reported by Graetzer 2012 p. 23: on alternate syllables after the initial one, excluding the final syllable (i.e. left-to-right trochaic alternation with final-syllable extrametricality). Not tested instrumentally (corpus is disyllabic).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Gupapuyngu. For the sibling Dhuwal varieties, Morphy 1983 (Djapu, p. 25) and Amery 1985 (Yirrkala Yolngu Matha, p. 36) say stress is 'almost always' initial with a handful of exceptions, chiefly words whose second syllable begins with /d/ (Morphy, citing Schebeck).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical stress). The instrumental corpus consists of isolated citation-form CV1.CV2 words, so word stress and phrasal (nuclear) accent coincide on the initial syllable; the 2014/2016 papers say this explicitly. The full alternating rule is Graetzer's report of Lowe's 1975 pedagogical pronunciation booklet, not an independent analysis; the first-hand element is the acoustic identification of the initial syllable as the stressed one.
new_statements.identity_note: Gupapuyngu (Gupapuyŋu, Gobabingo) is the western, Yirritja-moiety Dhuwala variety of Dhuwal-Dhuwala (Yolngu), spoken at Milingimbi, Ramingining, Gapuwiyak and Galiwin'ku. Graetzer's corpus: three adult female Gupapuyngu speakers (AM, BT, EG, aged 40-49) recorded by Andrew Butcher 1988-1991, community not stated. Lowe's 1975 booklet is Galiwin'ku/Milingimbi Gupapuyngu. The Djapu (Morphy 1983) and Yirrkala (Amery 1985) statements held by the project under guma1253 describe sibling Dhuwal varieties (Dhuwal = dhuw1249), not Gupapuyngu itself.
